nameStory: Five Angled Dodder gets its name from the five distinct angles on its tiny flowers, which help botanists tell it apart from its dodder cousins. The word 'dodder' comes from an old Germanic word meaning 'to tremble' - a perfect description of how these thread-like vines quiver in the breeze as they wrap around their host plants.
description: Five Angled Dodder is a parasitic vine that looks like bright orange or yellow spaghetti wrapped around other plants. This slender annual doesn't have normal green leaves - instead, it produces thin, twisting stems that coil around host plants and steal their nutrients through tiny suckers. The entire plant creates dense tangles that can cover shrubs and wildflowers like a colorful web, growing throughout the summer months.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Thread-like orange to yellow stems that twist and coil around host plants, creating dense tangles that feel smooth and slightly waxy to the touch

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Tiny white or cream-colored flowers in small clusters, each flower having five distinct angles when viewed closely - you'll need a hand lens to see this key feature clearly

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: No true leaves - just tiny, colorless scales that feel like small bumps along the smooth stems

idTips.label: Host Plants
idTips.description: Most commonly found wrapped around members of the aster family - look for it on goldenrods, asters, and other composite flowers in late summer

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Stems feel surprisingly firm and smooth, not sticky or rough, and break cleanly when pulled rather than stretching

habitat: Look for Five Angled Dodder in moist, open areas like riverbanks, wet meadows, and pond edges throughout New England. It tolerates disturbance well, so you might also spot it along roadsides, in old fields, or at the edges of wetlands where its favorite aster family hosts grow abundantly.

seasonality.spring: Seeds germinate in late spring, producing tiny seedlings that must quickly find a host plant or die within days.
seasonality.summer: Most visible from mid to late summer when bright orange tangles become obvious on host plants, with tiny flowers appearing in clusters.
seasonality.fall: Produces small round seeds before dying with the first frost, leaving brown, brittle stem remnants on host plants.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent - only seeds remain dormant in the soil waiting for spring warmth.

funFact: Five Angled Dodder seeds can lie dormant in soil for over 20 years, waiting for the perfect conditions to sprout - but once they germinate, they have only about 10 days to find a host plant before they starve to death!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with Field Dodder, but Five Angled Dodder prefers wetter habitats and has a strong preference for aster family plants, while Field Dodder attacks a wider variety of hosts in drier locations. Remember: wet areas and asters = five angled, dry fields and varied hosts = field dodder.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being parasitic, dodders are actually closely related to morning glories and are considered true flowering plants, not fungi or algae as many people assume when they first see these strange orange tangles.
compareHints: Five Angled Dodder is much rarer in New England than the common Scaldweed dodder, and prefers wetter habitats compared to Field Dodder's preference for dry agricultural areas. Unlike Buttonbush Dodder which specifically targets buttonbush shrubs, Five Angled Dodder focuses on herbaceous aster family plants in moist open areas.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Scaldweed differs from its dodder relatives primarily in where it grows - it prefers wetter habitats than Field Dodder, and its stems tend to be slightly thicker than Five Angled Dodder.
Compared to other dodders in New England, field dodder produces the largest seeds and tends to form denser, more tangled masses.

Buttonbush Dodder differs from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and host preferences - while Field Dodder attacks crops and Scaldweed Dodder prefers woodland edges, Buttonbush Dodder is the aquatic specialist of the family.
Lizard's tail dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its wetland habitat and highly specific host preference for lizard's tail plants.
Sessile Dodder is unique among New England dodders for specializing on woody hosts rather than soft-stemmed plants.
Smartweed Dodder is distinguished from other New England dodders primarily by its habitat and host preferences - it's the wetland specialist of the dodder family.
Among New England's dodder species, hazel dodder is distinguished by its preference for woody shrubs rather than herbaceous plants.
